pages.text: Dark storm clouds rolled across the afternoon sky as eleven-year-old Yaw walked to his mother’s tailoring shop carrying a sturdy yellow umbrella. Next door, Uncle Tetteh laughed from behind his provision counter. ‘Yaw, the sun was shining ten minutes ago! Why carry an umbrella before the rain starts?’ His mother, Auntie Akosua, smiled from her sewing machine. ‘Because once the storm is pouring, Uncle Tetteh, it is too late to go shopping for an umbrella!’

pages.alt: Eleven-year-old Yaw carries a bright yellow umbrella outside Auntie Akosua’s tailoring shop while dark rain clouds gather overhead.

pages.text: That night, a fierce rainstorm roared through the town. Wind rattled the shutters and heavy rain hammered the metal roofs. In the morning, Yaw and Auntie Akosua stepped outside and gasped. A fallen mango branch had cracked the corner of Auntie Akosua’s shop roof and also smashed the roof of Uncle Tetteh’s provision store next door, soaking sacks of rice and cartons of soap.

pages.alt: On the morning after the storm, a fallen tree branch rests across the damaged roofs of Auntie Akosua’s and Uncle Tetteh’s adjacent shops.

pages.text: Uncle Tetteh sat on a wooden crate with his head in his hands. ‘Fixing my roof and replacing the damaged goods will cost two thousand cedis,’ he whispered. ‘I only have four hundred cedis in my emergency savings, and I never signed up for shop insurance.’ Beside him, Auntie Akosua was also worried about her damaged roof, but she calmly opened a dry metal tin and took out her shop insurance policy document.

pages.text: ‘Mama, what is insurance, and how can a piece of paper fix a roof?’ asked Yaw. Auntie Akosua drew a big bowl on a piece of card. ‘Insurance works through risk pooling,’ she explained. ‘Imagine one hundred shopkeepers each pay a small regular amount, called a premium, of one hundred cedis a year into one shared protection pool. One hundred times one hundred cedis puts ten thousand cedis into the pool!’

‘Insurance works through risk pooling,’ she explained.

One hundred times one hundred cedis puts ten thousand cedis into the pool!’
pages.alt: Auntie Akosua draws a diagram showing 100 shopkeepers each placing 100 cedis into a 10,000-cedi shared protection pool.

pages.text: ‘In any single year,’ Auntie Akosua continued, ‘most of those one hundred shopkeepers will not have a tree fall on their roof. Suppose only two shops suffer heavy storm damage costing three thousand cedis each, six thousand cedis in total. Because all one hundred shopkeepers shared the risk in advance, the ten-thousand-cedi pool easily pays to repair both damaged shops, so no single family is ruined!’

pages.alt: The diagram shows the shared pool rebuilding two storm-damaged roofs while the other ninety-eight shops stay safe.

pages.text: That afternoon, Mrs Mensah, a licensed inspector from Auntie Akosua’s insurance company, arrived with her camera and clipboard. Auntie Akosua submitted a formal claim, a request asking the insurer to pay for a covered loss, along with photos of the fallen branch and the carpenter’s repair estimate of two thousand cedis. Mrs Mensah checked the policy rules carefully.

Auntie Akosua submitted a formal claim, a request asking the insurer to pay for a covered loss, along with photos of the fallen branch and the carpenter’s repair estimate of two thousand cedis.
Mrs Mensah checked the policy rules carefully.
pages.alt: Mrs Mensah inspects the damaged shop roof with a clipboard and camera while Auntie Akosua and Yaw show the carpenter’s estimate.

pages.text: ‘Your policy covers sudden storm damage,’ Mrs Mensah explained to Yaw, ‘and it has a two-hundred-cedi deductible, the small first portion of the repair cost that the policyholder pays from their own pocket. Since the carpenter’s repair costs two thousand cedis, you pay your two-hundred-cedi deductible from your emergency savings, and the insurance company pays the remaining one thousand eight hundred cedis!’

Since the carpenter’s repair costs two thousand cedis, you pay your two-hundred-cedi deductible from your emergency savings, and the insurance company pays the remaining one thousand eight hundred cedis!’
pages.alt: Mrs Mensah explains how the 2,000-cedi repair is split between the 200-cedi deductible and the 1,800-cedi insurance payout.

pages.text: ‘Does insurance pay for every single problem?’ asked Yaw. ‘No,’ said Mrs Mensah honestly. ‘Every policy has conditions and exclusions. It covers sudden, unexpected events listed in the contract, like storm or fire damage, not slow everyday wear and tear from rust, and never dishonest or fake claims! Also, in Ghana, always verify that an insurer is licensed by the National Insurance Commission, the NIC, so you know your claims will be honoured fairly.’

Also, in Ghana, always verify that an insurer is licensed by the National Insurance Commission, the NIC, so you know your claims will be honoured fairly.’
pages.alt: Mrs Mensah points to the official NIC licence seal and explains why honest claims and routine maintenance both matter.

pages.text: ‘Wait!’ said Yaw, remembering his family’s clinic cards. ‘Is the National Health Insurance Scheme, NHIS, also risk pooling?’ ‘Exactly!’ smiled Mrs Mensah. ‘Millions of Ghanaians contribute to the NHIS through taxes and membership renewals so that when anyone falls sick with malaria or needs covered hospital care, the shared pool helps pay the medical bills. Insurance works best alongside an emergency savings fund for deductibles and small daily needs.’

pages.text: By Friday, Auntie Akosua’s roof was gleaming and dry, and her sewing machines were humming again. Together with neighbours, she helped Uncle Tetteh repair his roof, and on Monday morning, Uncle Tetteh walked straight to an NIC-licensed office to register his shop and top up his emergency savings. He grinned at Yaw’s yellow umbrella. ‘From now on, Yaw, I buy my umbrella before the rain!’

activities.question: If 100 shopkeepers each pay a 100-cedi premium into a shared pool, how much is in the pool to cover two 3,000-cedi storm losses?
options: 10,000 cedis in the pool, which easily covers the 6,000 cedis in losses
1,000 cedis in the pool, which is not enough for one roof
100 cedis in total for the whole town
activities.explanation: 100 × 100 cedis = 10,000 cedis in the shared pool, enough to pay 2 × 3,000 = 6,000 cedis of storm repairs.

activities.definition: The regular payment made to keep an insurance policy active
distractors: A broken tree branch that falls during a thunderstorm
A prize given to people who never carry umbrellas

activities.question: Auntie Akosua’s covered roof repair cost 2,000 cedis and her policy had a 200-cedi deductible. How much did the insurer pay?
activities.explanation: Auntie Akosua paid her 200-cedi deductible from emergency savings, and the insurer paid 2,000 − 200 = 1,800 cedis.

activities.question: Which public body regulates and licenses insurance companies in Ghana?
activities.explanation: The National Insurance Commission (NIC) licenses and regulates insurers in Ghana to protect policyholders.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of how insurance protected Auntie Akosua’s shop in order.
items: Pay regular premiums into an NIC-licensed pool before any storm.
Submit an honest claim with photos and estimates after storm damage.
Pay the 200-cedi deductible while the pool pays 1,800 cedis.

activities.prompt: How did combining personal responsibility (insurance + emergency savings) with neighbourly kindness help the whole street recover?
